new_statements.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1968. Lexicostatistical study of the languages of Choiseul Island, British Solomon Islands. In A. Capell, G.J. Parker & A.J. Schütz (eds), Papers in Linguistics of Melanesia No. 1, 1-26. Pacific Linguistics A-15. Canberra: ANU. [= A's work 3, re-reported because it does carry a stress remark]
new_statements.locator: p. 2 (PDF p. 2), section 2 'Word lists', spelling note (3); Vangunu/Bareke forms checked on pp. 7-10 (Section II, items 1-100)
new_statements.check: not checked by the second reader
new_statements.relation_note: In the spelling conventions for the wordlists Capell states that stress is 'very frequently ante-penultimate' and that any stress liable to cause difficulty will be marked with an acute accent. On the New Georgia table (pp. 7-10) no Vangunu or Bareke form carries an acute (only the heading 'Kazúkuru'; Vangunu to:nganani has a length colon), so by the paper's convention no Vangunu/Bareke item is flagged as deviating -- but the remark is a blanket one over c. 14 languages' student-written lists, not a description of Vangunu stress, and 'very frequently' is not a rule. Weak, indirect evidence at most; I would not stage it as a Vangunu antepenultimate rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Blanket transcription note: across the vocabularies in this paper (which include the Vangunu and Bareke 100-word lists) stress falls 'very frequently' on the antepenultimate syllable; exceptional stresses to be marked with an acute; no Vangunu or Bareke form is so marked.
new_statements.exceptions: none marked for Vangunu or Bareke (acute accents promised for exceptional stress; none appear in their columns)
new_statements.identity_note: Section II wordlist (pp. 7-10) has separate 'Vangunu' and 'Bareke' columns (both vang1243) beside Mono, Hoava, Duke, Kazukuru; the p. 2 stress remark is a transcription note for ALL lists in the paper (Choiseul dialects, Mono, New Georgia languages, Kia), compiled by Methodist Goldie College students at Banga except Kia -- not phrased about Vangunu specifically.
